excerpt: When someone other than your employer caused a work injury, you may have a claim beyond workers' compensation. How the two fit together.

faqs.question: What is a third-party claim for a work injury?
faqs.answer: It is a claim against a person or company other than your employer who caused your accident. It is separate from your workers' compensation claim, and you can pursue both at the same time.

faqs.question: Why can't I sue my employer directly?
faqs.answer: Workers' compensation is a no-fault system that pays medical expenses and replaces part of your wages without you having to prove your employer was negligent. The trade-off is that injured employees are usually barred from suing their employer.

faqs.question: What are common examples of third-party liability at work?
faqs.answer: Car accidents while driving a company vehicle or performing work tasks, injuries from defective tools or equipment, construction site accidents caused by another subcontractor or an equipment company, and injuries on someone else's property while making a work call.

faqs.question: Can I claim against a general contractor if I work for a subcontractor?
faqs.answer: Usually not. In both Georgia and South Carolina, a general contractor is generally treated as your “statutory employer” and is protected from lawsuits the same way your own employer is (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-8; S.C. Code § 42-1-415). Another subcontractor, an equipment maker, or a property owner who is not a contractor on the job can often be sued.

faqs.question: Do I lose my workers' compensation benefits if I bring a third-party claim?
faqs.answer: No. A third-party claim runs alongside your workers' compensation claim rather than replacing it. The two have different targets, different standards of proof, and different types of recoverable damages. Your workers' compensation insurer may, however, be repaid out of what you recover from the third party.

metaDescription: Hurt at work by someone other than your employer? Learn how a third-party claim works alongside workers' comp in Georgia and South Carolina.
